text: Darwin is the core Unix-like operating system underlying macOS, iOS, watchOS, tvOS, iPadOS, audioOS, visionOS, and bridgeOS. It was initially released as an independent open-source operating system by Apple in 2000 and is composed of code derived from NeXTSTEP, FreeBSD, and other BSD operating systems, Mach, and other free software projects, as well as code developed by Apple. Darwin's unofficial mascot is Hexley the Platypus. It is mostly POSIX-compatible but has never been certified as compliant with any version of POSIX; however, starting with Leopard, macOS has been certified as compatible with the Single UNIX Specification version 3 (SUSv3). The heritage of Darwin traces back to Unix derivatives enhanced by NeXTSTEP (later known as OPENSTEP, from version 4.0 onward), first released in 1989. After Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it announced it would base its next operating system on OPENSTEP, which evolved into Rhapsody in 1997, Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999, Mac OS X Public Beta in 2000, and Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. In 1999, Apple announced the release of the Mach 2.5 microkernel, BSD Unix 4.4 OS, and Apache Web server components of Mac OS X Server. At that time, interim CEO Steve Jobs referenced British naturalist Charles Darwin by saying "because it's about evolution." In 2000, the core operating system components of Mac OS X were released as open-source software under the Apple Public Source License (APSL) as Darwin, while higher-level components like Cocoa and Carbon frameworks remained closed-source. Up to Darwin 8.0.1, released in April 2005, Apple provided a binary installer (as an ISO image) after each major Mac OS X release to allow installation of Darwin as a standalone operating system on PowerPC and Intel x86 systems; minor updates were distributed as separate packages. Darwin is now only available as source code, and as of January 2023, Apple no longer mentions Darwin by name on its Open Source website, publishing only an incomplete collection of open-source projects related to macOS and iOS. The kernel of Darwin is XNU, a hybrid kernel using Open Software Foundation Mach Kernel (OSFMK) 7.3 from the OSF, elements of FreeBSD (including the process model, network stack, and virtual file system), and an object-oriented device driver API called IOKit, providing the flexibility of a microkernel and the performance of a monolithic kernel. The last bootable full release of Darwin supported 32-bit and 64-bit Apple PowerPC systems and 32-bit Intel PCs. Darwin currently supports the 64-bit x86-64 variant of Intel x86 processors in Intel-based Macs and 64-bit ARM processors in the iPhone 5S and later, the 6th generation iPod Touch, the 5th generation iPad and later, the iPad Air family, the iPad Mini 2 and later, the iPad Pro family, the fourth generation and later Apple TVs, the HomePod family, and Macs with Apple silicon such as the 2020 Apple M1 Macs, as well as the Raspberry Pi 3B. An open-source port of the XNU kernel exists for Intel and AMD x86 platforms not officially supported by Apple, though it has not been updated since 2009, and another exists for ARM platforms, though it has not been updated since 2016. Older versions supported some or all of 32-bit PowerPC, 64-bit PowerPC, 32-bit x86, and 32-bit ARM. Darwin supports the POSIX API through its BSD lineage (largely FreeBSD userland), enabling many programs written for other UNIX-like systems to be compiled without source code changes. Darwin does not include key macOS components such as the Carbon and Cocoa APIs or the Quartz Compositor and Aqua user interface, so it cannot run Mac applications, though it does support lesser-known macOS features like mDNSResponder (a core component of Bonjour) and launchd (an advanced service management framework). In July 2003, Apple released Darwin under version 2.0 of the APSL, which the Free Software Foundation (FSF) qualifies as a free software license. The APSL is similar to AGPL and is incompatible with the GNU General Public License. Earlier versions of the APSL did not meet the FSF's definition of free software, though they met the Open Source Definition. A table of major Darwin releases with their dates and corresponding derivative operating system releases is provided, noting that OS releases may have been issued on different dates. The version jump from Darwin 1.4.1 to 5.1 with the release of Mac OS X v10.1.1 was designed to align Darwin with the Mac OS X version and build numbering system, inherited from NeXTSTEP. In macOS build numbering, each version has a unique beginning build number identifying the whole version (e.g., Mac OS X v10.0 started with build numbers beginning at 4, v10.1 began at 5). Build dates for Darwin versions are not publicly available; the command `uname -r` shows the Darwin version number (e.g., "20.3.0"), and `uname -v` shows the XNU build version string including the Darwin version number. The command `sw_vers` displays the corresponding ProductName ("macOS"), ProductVersion ("11.2.3"), and BuildVersion ("20D91"). Due to Darwin's free software nature, various projects have aimed to modify the system or use its components. Among these, DarwinBSD, OpenDarwin, and PureDarwin are considered "alternative Darwin distributions" akin to Linux distributions. OpenDarwin was a community-led operating system based on Darwin, founded in April 2002 by Apple and the Internet Systems Consortium, aiming to foster collaboration between Apple developers and the free software community. Apple benefited from incorporating OpenDarwin improvements into Darwin releases, and the community gained control over its own operating system for use in distributions like GNU-Darwin. On July 25, 2006, the OpenDarwin team announced the project's shutdown, citing that it had "become a mere hosting facility for Mac OS X related projects" and that efforts to create a standalone Darwin OS had failed. Contributing factors included the unavailability of sources, limited interaction with Apple, difficulty building and tracking sources, and lack of community interest. The last stable release was version 7.2.1, released on July 16, 2004. PureDarwin is a project to create a bootable operating system image from Apple's released Darwin source code. Since the closure of OpenDarwin and the release of bootable images from Darwin 8.x, creating a full operating system has become increasingly difficult due to many components becoming closed source. In 2015, PureDarwin released a preview based on Darwin 9 with an X11 GUI, followed by a command-line-only 17.4 Beta based on Darwin 17 in 2019. Other projects are categorized as "Darwin distributions" or alternative derivatives. Some projects re-implement parts of macOS APIs above the level of Darwin, but are not considered Darwin derivatives beyond the extent that such programs are derived from operating system application programming interfaces and constraints.
